claims.text: An empirical study of open-source pull request workflows found that specification quality does not predict defects (p = 0.164) or rework (p = 0.860).
The same study found that specifications do not constrain the scope of AI-tagged changes (p = 0.997).
The study concludes that specification artifacts proxy for task complexity rather than quality improvement.
The study's sample contained no repository that commits actual SDD tool output, so SDD tool adoption itself remains untested.
The study states that no SDD tool vendor has published empirical evidence for its quality claims.
In the study, pull requests referencing a tracking issue made up 97.5% of the treatment group, which the authors say is not equivalent to Spec Kit or Kiro's guided-workflow output.
GitHub's Spec Kit blog claims that a clear specification up front, with a technical plan and focused tasks, gives the coding agent more clarity and improves its efficacy.
Kiro claims specifications enable fewer iterations and higher accuracy.
Böckeler defines spec-driven development as writing a spec before writing code with AI, where the spec becomes the source of truth for the human and the AI.
Spec Kit's template asks for core requirements, acceptance criteria, edge cases, data models, API contracts and user stories.
Kiro stores each feature's spec as three Markdown files in a per-feature folder under .kiro/specs/: requirements.md, design.md and tasks.md.
Kiro requirements.md uses numbered '### Requirement N' blocks, each with one user story and numbered EARS acceptance criteria, addressed as <requirement>.<criterion> (e.g. 1.2).
Kiro uses EARS patterns (event-driven WHEN, conditional IF, compound WHEN...AND, continuous WHILE, contextual WHERE), each ending in a SHALL response.
Kiro's generated design.md has sections in order: Overview, Architecture (often Mermaid diagrams), Components and Interfaces, Data Models, Error Handling, Testing Strategy.

Kiro's tasks.md is a numbered checkbox list titled 'Implementation Plan', at most two levels deep, with decimal sub-tasks (1.1, 1.2) and a final '_Requirements: …_' bullet back-referencing requirement criteria, giving task-to-requirement traceability.
Kiro's agent is instructed to keep tasks to coding work only (no deploy, metrics or manual QA tasks).
Kiro steering files (product.md, tech.md, structure.md) under .kiro/steering/ provide project-wide context alongside specs.
In Kiro's default Requirements-First workflow the user reviews and approves each file before the next is generated; Design-First derives requirements from the design instead.

Kiro recommends Design-First when an existing architecture exists, strict non-functional requirements (latency, throughput, compliance) apply, or technical feasibility is being explored; Requirements-First suits known behavior with flexible architecture.

Kiro's 'Analyze Requirements' feature runs a deep analysis to catch logical inconsistencies, ambiguities, conflicting constraints and gaps, and 'Sync Files' on tasks.md creates new tasks after requirements or design change.
When running all tasks, Kiro builds a dependency graph of tasks in tasks.md and groups independent tasks into waves; waves run sequentially while tasks within a wave run concurrently.
Kiro bugfix specs use bugfix.md in place of requirements.md, capturing current, expected and unchanged behavior.
Kiro's Quick Spec mode asks clarifying questions up front and then auto-generates requirements.md, design.md and tasks.md in sequence with no approval gates between phases.
Kiro recommends committing spec files under .kiro/specs to the repo alongside code so they serve as a record of intent and design for future developers and for Kiro.
Kiro's EARS requirements follow the pattern 'WHEN [condition/event] THE SYSTEM SHALL [expected behavior]', claimed to give clarity, testability, traceability and completeness.
